definition: A strong desire to do or achieve something.
examples: Macbeth’s ambition to become king drives him to murder Duncan.
Lady Macbeth’s ambition is just as strong as her husband’s.
Walton’s ambition makes him say “one man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the knowledge which I sought”.

definition: A character flaw that leads to their downfall in a tragedy.
examples: Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s hamartia as his over-ambitious nature.
If it was not for his hamartia, Macbeth would not have had a downfall.

definition: Make secret plans with someone to commit a harmful act.
examples: Witches are conspiring to destroy the natural order.
In Jacobean times, people feared that witches might conspire against the King.

definition: Someone who uses underhand tactics to harm, trick or lead others astray.
examples: Witches are devious creatures.
Witches use devious methods to corrupt innocent people.

definition: When someone or something seems to represent what it means to be “manly”.
examples: When the Captain describes Macbeth, he seems to be an embodiment of masculinity.
Macbeth is an embodiment of masculinity because he is a brave and fearless fighter in battle.

definition: A character who begins the play in a position of high status in society and is deeply respected by others, but who has a hamartia (fatal flaw) that leads to their downfall.
A Scottish lord.
An unavoidable future that you cannot control.
examples: After the prophecy, Macbeth’s fate was sealed.

definition: The power to choose your own path without influence.
examples: Macbeth acts of his own free will when he chooses to murder Duncan.
The witches predict the future, but they never force Macbeth to use his free will for evil.

definition: Something that is unavoidable.
examples: After the witches’ prophecy, Macbeth’s downfall seems inevitable.
As a tragic hero, Macbeth’s fall is inevitable because of his hamartia.

definition: A prediction of what will happen in the future.
Something that prompts and encourages the events to happen.
examples: The witches are a catalyst for Macbeth’s downfall.
Macbeth’s ambition is a catalyst for his downfall because it encourages him to commit evil acts of violence.

definition: Going against what you expect of how men or women should behave.
examples: The witches are presented as women, but Shakespeare subverts gender expectations because they have beards too.
Women in Jacobean times were expected to be submissive and gentle, so women who were dominant and strong subverted the expectations of gender.

definition: Lying or tricking someone.
examples: Macbeth’s deception is when he hides his violent ambition from the characters around him.
Banquo does not trust the witches and he believes they are being deceptive.

definition: Giving a false outward appearance.
topic: Deception; Sin; Façades; Set and Stage Directions
examples: Lady Macbeth tells her husband to put on a façade of friendliness when Duncan arrives at the castle.
Macbeth keeps up a façade of grief after the murder, even though he killed Duncan.

definition: The belief that God has chosen and anointed the King to rule.
examples: Many Jacobeans believed in the Divine Right to Rule, the belief that the King was chosen by God. This meant an act against the king was an act against God.

definition: The belief that a host should guard and protect their guests from harm.
examples: Medieval society believed in the Duties of Hospitality, the belief that a host should guard and protect their guests. This meant if a host betrayed their duties, they were committing a terrible sin.

definition: A speech where the character expresses their inner thoughts and feelings to the audience.
A relative.
Make a man feel like they are not “manly” enough.
examples: Lady Macbeth emasculates her husband when she commands him to do what she tells him.
It is ironic that Macbeth feels emasculated by his wife because others view him as an embodiment of masculinity.

definition: Make someone feel small and worthless.
examples: Lady Macbeth belittles her husband by suggesting he is weak and unable to commit the murder like he promised.
It is ironic that Macbeth feels belittled because he is a powerful and respected thane who others admire and look up to.

definition: Seeing something that is not real but is created by the mind.
examples: The floating dagger could be a hallucination created by Macbeth’s guilty mind.
Banquo’s ghost may be a hallucination because only Macbeth can see it.

definition: Using magic to make something appear in physical form.
examples: The witches conjured an evil spirit to haunt the poor girl and her family.

definition: Feeling overwhelmed by an emotion, like it is swallowing you.
examples: In the poem ‘Bayonet Charge’, the soldier is consumed by his fear and trauma.

definition: Trying to stop or hide an emotion by burying it deep down.
examples: Lady Macbeth tries to suppress her guilt by saying “A little water clears us of this deed”.
In Act 5, Macbeth tries to suppress his fear by telling himself he bears a charmed life.

definition: The way things should naturally be in the universe.
examples: When Duncan is king, the natural order is maintained.
By murdering Duncan, Macbeth breaks the natural order.

definition: Something that is magical and unnatural.
Feeling like people are trying to get you, making you scared and suspicious.
examples: Macbeth becomes paranoid that Banquo will betray him.
Paranoid about losing the crown, Macbeth sends murderers to kill Banquo and Fleance.

definition: This establishes the tragic hero and their hamartia.
Here the situation worsens because of the early decisions of the tragic hero.
This is the turning point where the tragic hero’s plans go wrong.
examples: A pivotal moment is when Victor creates the monster. Before, he was full of excitement and ambition, but after he was horrified.
A pivotal moment is when William is murdered because Victor realises there are terrible consequences for his actions.

definition: This shows the gradual downfall of the tragic hero.
Here the tragic hero finally suffers their tragic fate, usually death.
examples: Sheila and Eric want a resolution in which the family accepts responsibility, but their parents refuse.
Priestley does not give the audience a neat resolution at the end of the play.

definition: Giving something a physical form or body.
topic: Banquo’s Ghost; Mr Utterson; The True Monster
examples: Banquo’s ghost is the embodiment of Macbeth’s guilt.
Lady Macbeth wants to become the embodiment of cruelty when she asks the spirits to “unsex” her.
William is an embodiment of innocence and purity.
The De Lacey family are an embodiment of a kind and loving family.

definition: This is when you know a prediction of the future, and by knowing it, you cause it to happen.
examples: Some people argue that the witches’ prophecy is a self-fulfilling prophecy because Macbeth murders Duncan to make it come true.
If Macbeth had not believed the prophecy, he might never have killed Duncan, so it could be a self-fulfilling prophecy.

definition: A cruel ruler who has too much power.
examples: By the end of the play, Macbeth is a tyrant who orders the murder of Macduff’s family.
Malcolm calls Macbeth a “tyrant” because he rules through violence and fear.

definition: The belief that a country is like a physical body, with the King being the head of the body.
examples: In Jacobean times, some believed in the body politic, meaning they thought that if the King was a tyrant, the whole country would suffer.

definition: This is when your mind begins to “unravel” and fall apart.
examples: The character in ‘Poppies’ experiences a psychological unravelling when her son is killed in conflict.
The murder of Duncan caused a psychological unravelling of Macbeth.

definition: Feeling overconfident.
examples: Macbeth’s hubris grows when he believes that no man “of woman born” can harm him.
His hubris in Act 5 makes him ignore the danger of Macduff.

definition: No longer feeling shock, after experiencing something shocking or upsetting many times.
examples: By Act 5, Macbeth is desensitised to fear and says he has “almost forgot the taste of fears”.
Macbeth becomes desensitised to violence as he orders more and more murders.

definition: Describes a person who believes that life has no meaning or purpose.
examples: Macbeth sounds nihilistic when he describes life as “signifying nothing”.
After Lady Macbeth’s death, Macbeth feels nihilistic and believes that life has no meaning.

definition: When a tragic hero realises something shocking, usually when it is too late to change his fate.
examples: Macbeth experiences anagnorisis when he learns that Macduff was “untimely ripped” from his mother’s womb.
His anagnorisis comes too late to change his fate.

definition: The belief that life has no meaning or purpose.
A society ruled and controlled by men.
The story is told in third person (he/she), but the narrator tells it from the point of view of a character.
examples: Stevenson writes in third-person limited and the reader sees the events through Mr Utterson’s eyes.

definition: The voice that tells the story. It refers to who is telling the events, how much they know, and how the story is presented to the reader.
examples: Stevenson uses a third-person narrator to tell the story.

definition: The technique by which a narrative presents information through a specific focal character or viewpoint.
examples: Because events are focalised through Utterson, the reader discovers the truth slowly, building suspense.

definition: Getting enjoyment from watching someone else do something.
examples: Utterson gets vicarious pleasure from watching his friends give in to temptation, because he refuses to do so himself.
The reader gets vicarious pleasure from the mystery as Utterson hunts for Hyde.

definition: Having two opposite sides.
examples: Stevenson describes the duality of London. It is respectable and yet under the surface it is dangerous.
In Chapter One, Stevenson emphasises the dual nature of London.

definition: The study of a person’s facial appearance to understand their personality.
Go beyond the limits of what is morally, socially, or legally acceptable.
examples: Some Victorians believed that some science was transgressing the laws of nature.
Some Victorians believed that it was morally wrong for humans to transgress the laws of nature.

definition: A genre that follows a rational detective solving a crime.
examples: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is like a detective novel because Utterson investigates who Mr Hyde really is.
Like a detective novel, the story reveals the truth slowly, through clues such as the letter and the handwriting.

definition: A genre of literature that often explores fears, the way the past haunts the present and may include the supernatural.
examples: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is Gothic literature because it explores fear, the supernatural and the dark side of London.
Hyde’s sinister house and the foggy streets create the unsettling atmosphere of Gothic literature.
‘Frankenstein’ is Gothic because it has a monster, an isolated setting, a sense of mystery and characters turned mad.

definition: An essential characteristic or feature.
examples: Stevenson suggests that all humans have an inherent evil within them.

definition: Going against religious laws and beliefs.
examples: Saskia is a heretic because she wants to learn witchcraft.

definition: Analysing handwriting to determine someone’s personality traits.
examples: Mr Guest uses graphology when he notices that Jekyll’s handwriting looks like Hyde’s.
Graphology suggests that the matching handwriting reveals a link between the minds of Jekyll and Hyde.

definition: Describes the long-lasting shock caused by a disturbing experience.
examples: Dr Lanyon is traumatised after he sees Hyde transform into Jekyll.
Lanyon’s pale face and “deep-seated terror” show how traumatised he is.
Victor is traumatised by all he has seen, which is why Walton notices his “wildness, and even madness”.

definition: Wrath, lust, greed, gluttony, pride, envy and sloth.
The opposite of a sin.
A concept describing what is repulsive, degraded, or expelled to maintain personal identity or social rules. It provokes disgust and fascination.
examples: Hyde embodies the abject: his appearance and actions blur the lines between man and beast, morality and depravity.

definition: Describes something evil, like the Devil (Satan).
examples: Victorian society was strictly Christian and therefore would have feared satanic practices.

definition: When a writer describes something in a way that makes it seem like Hell.
examples: Stevenson uses hellish imagery when he describes Jekyll’s cabinet, with its “red baize door”.
The hellish imagery of the barred windows makes the cabinet seem like a prison of suffering.

definition: Something religious.
Saying something disrespectful about God.
A story that is written in the style of diaries, letters or newspaper articles.
examples: Chapter 9 of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is epistolary because it is Dr Lanyon’s letter.
The epistolary ending splits the narrative into letters, just as Jekyll splits himself in two.

definition: Being physically and mentally dependent on something.
examples: Jekyll’s addiction to becoming Hyde grows until he can no longer control it.
Jekyll says that his “new power tempted me until I fell into slavery”, which shows how addiction takes over.

definition: Reverting to a more primitive or animalistic state.
Understanding the difference between right and wrong behaviour.
examples: Mr Birling shows little morality when he sacks Eva Smith for asking for higher pay.
The Inspector tries to teach the Birlings a stronger sense of morality.

definition: The stage scenery and props used to create a scene.
examples: The set is a comfortable dining room full of expensive furniture, which suggests the Birlings’ wealth.
The set includes a small table with a telephone, which is used in the ending.

definition: The descriptions in the play explaining what happens on stage. This includes the lighting, set changes and costumes.
examples: The stage directions say the lighting changes from “pink and intimate” to “brighter and harder” when the Inspector arrives.
Stage directions such as “cutting in, massively” show how the Inspector takes control.

definition: When you see things in a happy and romantic way that is not the truth.
When the audience knows something that the characters do not.
examples: Mr Birling’s claim that the Titanic is “unsinkable” is dramatic irony, because the 1945 audience knows that it sank.
Birling’s confidence that there will be no war creates dramatic irony for an audience who had lived through two world wars.

definition: Lacking knowledge or awareness.
examples: Mr Birling is ignorant of the future when he says the Titanic is unsinkable.
The Birlings are ignorant of how their actions affected Eva Smith.

definition: Look at closely to assess the condition and to discover any flaws.
examples: The Inspector inspects the Birlings’ lives closely and uncovers their secrets.
Inspector Goole inspects each character’s part in Eva Smith’s death.

definition: All powerful.
examples: The Inspector seems omnipotent because he has a powerful presence that intimidates the Birling family.

definition: All knowing.
examples: The Inspector seems omniscient because he seems to know everything about the Birlings, including their deepest secrets.

definition: An economic system where people own their own property and business.
examples: Mr Birling believes in capitalism and thinks that a man has to “look after himself and his own”.
Priestley uses Mr Birling to show the greed of capitalism.

definition: An economic system where the rich help the poor to better the whole of society.
examples: The Inspector represents socialism when he says “We are members of one body”.
Priestley wrote the play because he believed in socialism.

definition: Using someone for your own benefit, often treating them like an object.
examples: Mr Birling shows how many capitalists will happily exploit their workers.
Eva Smith is the victim of exploitation.

definition: A message that uses the characters to make a strongly worded criticism of society.
A system where society is organised into different classes.
examples: The class system separates the wealthy Birlings from working-class people like Eva Smith.
Mrs Birling’s snobbery shows how the class system shaped attitudes in 1912.

definition: Being fragile and at risk of harm.
examples: Eva Smith is vulnerable because she has no family to help her.
Eva is vulnerable because she depends on her job to survive.

definition: Having your power taken away.
examples: Eva is disempowered because Mr Birling can sack her for asking for more money.
Women in 1912 were often disempowered by a patriarchal society.

definition: Those with the most power and wealth. Often these are aristocracy who have inherited land and titles.
Those with some power and wealth. They have professional jobs, often working in business, and often enjoy privileges and opportunities not available to the working class.
People with low-paying jobs, often manual work. These are often the poorest people in society.
An immoral act against God.
examples: Mr Birling is sinful for keeping his money all to himself.

definition: A medieval play that taught the audience how to be good people.
To use or take advantage of someone (verb).
examples: Mr Birling exploits the working class to make as much money as he can.
Priestley highlights how the exploitation of the working class is unfair and immoral.

definition: To treat someone disrespectfully and make them feel inferior.
examples: Mrs Birling degrades Eva by calling her “a girl of that sort”.
Mr Birling degrades his workers by treating them as “cheap labour”.

definition: Wants things in society to change and improve for the better.
examples: Priestley’s socialist views were very progressive.

definition: Wants things in society to stay the same and resists change.
examples: Mr Birling has conservative views because he wants society to stay the way it is.
Mrs Birling’s conservative attitudes make her refuse to help Eva Smith.

definition: Judging someone based upon bias without proper reasons or evidence (a thought).
examples: Mrs Birling’s class prejudice makes her assume that Eva is lying.
The Inspector challenges the Birlings’ prejudice against the working class.

definition: Treating someone differently and unfairly due to a prejudiced view (an action).
examples: Eva Smith experiences discrimination because of her class and her gender.
Mrs Birling discriminates against Eva by refusing her help at the charity.

definition: Using your power unfairly to mistreat or hurt others.
examples: Mr Birling abuses his power when he sacks Eva Smith for asking for higher pay.
Sheila abuses her power when she gets Eva dismissed from Milwards because she is jealous.

definition: Taking responsibility for something and accepting that you have a duty to take care of it.
examples: Sheila feels accountable for getting Eva Smith dismissed from Milwards.
Mr Birling refuses to be held accountable for what happened to Eva Smith.

definition: When the story ends with things being unresolved, often finishing with a dramatic moment.
examples: An Inspector Calls ends with a cliff-hanger when the telephone rings to say a girl has died and an inspector is on his way.
The final phone call is a cliff-hanger because we do not know what will happen to the Birlings.

definition: When the ending links in some way to the beginning of the story.
examples: The ending of An Inspector Calls feels like a circular narrative because another inspector is about to arrive, just as the first one did.
A circular narrative suggests that the Birlings may face the same questions again.

definition: Pointless and meaningless (adjective).
examples: Some war poets explore the futility of conflict in their poems.

definition: People who are sent to their deaths by being told to charge at the enemy’s cannons.
examples: In ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’, the soldiers are treated as cannon-fodder when they ride into the valley because of a mistake.
The Light Brigade are cannon-fodder because someone had blundered.

definition: A narrative poem often spoken aloud (usually to remember famous tragedies, battles or heroes).
Discovering something is not as good as you thought.
examples: I always dreamed of going to USA, but I became disillusioned when I got there and experienced many rude Americans.

definition: A psychological condition caused by a traumatic event. Long after the event, the person experiences intense, disturbing thoughts and emotions.
examples: The soldier in ‘Remains’ suffers from PTSD because he cannot forget the looter he shot.
Armitage suggests PTSD when the speaker says “But I blink and he bursts again”.

definition: Having a misplaced belief in things that are clearly not true.
Pride and love for one’s country.
Love for one’s country to an extreme (to the detriment of other nations).
Something you can throw away or dispose of easily.
examples: The pilot in ‘Kamikaze’ is treated as disposable by those who command him.
The soldiers in ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’ are disposable to their commanders.

definition: Repeating a belief to someone until they accept it without question.
examples: The pilot in ‘Kamikaze’ has been indoctrinated with patriotic ideas, shown by the “powerful incantations”.
The soldier in ‘Bayonet Charge’ was indoctrinated by propaganda to believe that war was glorious.

definition: A turning point in a poem.
examples: Many poets create a volta to show the way that a character changes.
Samantha thought that the beginning of the poem was dark and depressing but after the volta it became hopeful.

definition: Feeling like you are in the presence of a higher or greater power. It is so great and powerful it is difficult to fully understand.
examples: The speaker in ‘The Prelude’ experiences the sublime when the mountain towers above him.
Wordsworth shows the sublime power of nature through the “huge and mighty forms”.

definition: A collection of philosophers, writers and artists in the later 18th century who had shared ideas about humanity and society: nature is supreme, people should follow their emotions and imagination, and people should not be controlled but should be free.
examples: Mary Shelley’s own husband, Percy Bysshe Shelley, wrote many famous works of the Romantic Movement, including ‘Ozymandias’ and ‘Prometheus Unbound’.

definition: A long narrative poem that tells the story of a hero’s journey as they embark on a grand adventure.
A person who has once served in the army and has experienced conflict.
examples: The speaker in ‘Remains’ is a war veteran haunted by a memory.
Armitage gives a voice to war veterans in ‘Remains’.

definition: A photographer who takes images to be used by the news to tell the news story.
examples: Jerica was a photojournalist who had taken many powerful images of the wars she had witnessed in her career.

definition: Sharing part-responsibility for wrong-doing with other people.
examples: In ‘War Photographer’, the readers who ignore the suffering in the photographs are complicit.
The photographer may feel complicit because he earns his living from other people’s suffering.

definition: Not feeling concerned or interested in something.
examples: Duffy suggests apathy when she writes that “they do not care”.
The apathy of the people reading the newspaper contrasts with the photographer’s trauma.

definition: Deep sadness caused by loss, often someone’s death.
examples: The mother in ‘Poppies’ is consumed by grief for her son.
Weir shows her grief through the image of “spasms of paper red”.

definition: Something weak that can be easily broken and destroyed.
examples: The poet conveys the fragility of human life when he describes how easily the looter was killed in ‘Remains’.

definition: All things (moments, emotions, life and objects) are temporary, fleeting and constantly changing.
Being unfairly treated or controlled by someone with more power.
examples: Blake shows the oppression of ordinary people in ‘London’ through the “mind-forg’d manacles”.
Agard explores oppression through education in ‘Checking Out Me History’.

definition: Where a country takes control over the native people of an area.
examples: ‘Checking Out Me History’ is about the effects of colonisation on Caribbean identity.
Agard explores how Britain’s colonisation controlled what the speaker was taught.

definition: Soldiers directly involved in the fighting.
Other people affected by war who are not soldiers.
Emotional shock caused by distressing events.
Feeling responsible for wrongdoing.
A struggle between opposing forces.
Control or influence over others.
Sense of self shaped by experiences.
How past experiences are remembered (often distorted).
Consequences that affect people not directly involved.
The belief that nature is powerful and should be respected.
To steal the powers of a God.
examples: Prometheus appropriates divine power when he steals the fire from Zeus.
In ‘Frankenstein’, Shelley suggests that appropriating divine power could lead to terrible consequences.

definition: A story within a story.
examples: Shelley creates a frame narrative, starting with Walton’s story and then changing to Frankenstein’s story.
The frame narrative emphasises how Walton and Frankenstein are similar.

definition: Feeling like you deserve special treatment or privileges.
examples: Victor’s parents treat him as their “plaything and their idol”, which may have made him entitled.

definition: Believing that you are better than others.
examples: Victor’s sense of superiority grows because his parents treat him like a God.

definition: Wanting to achieve great scientific discoveries.
examples: Victor’s scientific ambition drives him to “pursue nature to her hiding places”.

definition: Having power or control without any limits.
examples: Victor wants absolute power over life and death when he hopes “a new species would bless me as its creator”.

definition: Pushing someone out of the role they should have.
examples: By creating life, Victor tries to displace God, and also displaces women, who normally give birth.

definition: Push someone to the edge of society, making them feel powerless.
examples: The villagers marginalise the Creature by attacking him without trying to speak to him.

definition: Being lonely and separated from others.
examples: The creature experiences physical isolation because he is cut off from others inside his hovel.
The creature experiences emotional isolation because there is no one who will show him love.
The creature feels isolated.

definition: The way a person sees themselves.
examples: Victor Frankenstein’s sense of self is influenced by his parents who spoil him and treat him like a God.
The deaths of William and Justine change Victor’s sense of self because he now sees himself as “the true murderer”.

definition: Treat someone as though they’re not human.
examples: Victor Frankenstein dehumanises his creation by refusing to give him a name.
Shelley suggests that the monster is dehumanised and rejected by Frankenstein.
Victor dehumanises the creature when he calls him a “vile insect”.

definition: The Age of Enlightenment was a period of scientific discovery and the development of knowledge from the end of the 1600s until 1815.
examples: In the Age of Enlightenment, medicine and technology developed at a rapid pace, which is the world Victor grows up in.

definition: A story that warns us of the dangers of doing something, such as transgressing the laws of nature in the hunt for divine power.
examples: ‘Frankenstein’ is a cautionary tale because it warns readers about the dangers of scientific ambition.

definition: The use of symbolism and strong images to allow the reader to picture what is described. It includes similes, metaphors and personification.
examples: Shelley uses nightmarish imagery such as “demoniacal corpse” to describe the Creature’s birth.

definition: An important project.
examples: Walton’s enterprise is to sail to the North Pole.

definition: Place that’s empty, ruined or destroyed.
examples: Walton imagines a land of beauty, not desolation.

definition: Place where you’re alone.
examples: Walton sails through “undiscovered solitudes”.

definition: Satisfy your desire.
examples: Walton’s voyage will not satiate his thirst for glory.

definition: Takes lots of hard work.
examples: Victor’s experiments were a laborious task.

definition: Completely surrounded.
examples: Walton’s ship is encompassed by ice.

definition: Attacked.
examples: Walton’s crew are assailed by storms and ice.

definition: Feeling something with extreme sadness or hatred.
examples: Walton bitterly feels the want of a friend.

definition: Extremely thin and weak.
examples: Victor’s “body dreadfully emaciated” shows how he has suffered.

definition: Tiredness and exhaustion.
examples: Victor collapses from fatigue after the chase over the ice.

definition: A person’s skeletal structure that is weak and crippled.
examples: Victor’s decaying frame is the first thing Walton notices.

definition: Walking for pleasure (usually in the countryside).
examples: As a child, Victor enjoyed rambles in the Swiss countryside.

definition: Never runs out.
examples: Victor’s parents had inexhaustible love for him.

definition: Lovingly touch or stroke.
examples: Victor remembers “my mother’s tender caresses”.

definition: All loving.
examples: Victor’s parents are benevolent and gentle towards him.

definition: Something you love and admire.
examples: Victor’s parents treat him as their “idol”.

definition: A strong enthusiasm.
examples: Victor has a fervent longing to learn nature’s secrets.

definition: A deep desire.
examples: Victor describes a “fervent longing to penetrate the secrets of nature”.

definition: Break into something, usually with a sharp point.
examples: Victor wants to penetrate nature’s secrets.

definition: Impossible to hurt.
examples: Victor imagines creating a species that is invulnerable to disease.

definition: Lead people to explore something new.
examples: Victor wants to pioneer a new kind of science.

definition: A building that stores dead bodies or skeletons.
examples: Victor collects body parts from charnel-houses.

definition: Handed down something that someone no longer uses.
examples: Victor’s materials are inherited from the dead.

definition: Treating something holy and sacred with disrespect.
examples: Victor profanes the human body for his experiment.

definition: Does not feel it.
examples: Victor becomes insensible to the horror of his work.

definition: The laws of nature that can never be changed.
examples: Victor breaks the immutable laws of nature.

definition: Peaceful and calm.
examples: The lake at Geneva looks serene before the storm.

definition: Pure and extreme joy.
examples: Victor watches the storm with ecstasy.

definition: Heavily bruised.
examples: William’s neck is livid from the murderer’s grasp.

definition: Small painting of someone’s face.
examples: William’s miniature of his mother is stolen.

definition: Escape being captured.
examples: The Creature seems able to elude all pursuit.

definition: Put into something.
examples: Victor tries to infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing.

definition: Sudden, violent shaking.
examples: The Creature’s limbs move with a convulsive motion.

definition: Softly shining (reflects light without glittering).
examples: Victor chose lustrous black hair for the Creature.

definition: Unclear words/sounds, unable to communicate.
examples: The Creature mutters “inarticulate sounds”.

definition: Possessed by a demon.
examples: Victor calls the Creature a “demoniacal corpse”.

definition: Someone unhappy, unfortunate, or disgusting.
examples: The Creature calls himself wretched.

definition: Seriously and badly.
examples: The villagers grievously injured the Creature.

definition: Find safety from harm.
examples: The Creature takes refuge in a hovel.

definition: A small, poor and dirty shelter.
examples: The Creature calls his hovel “my kennel”.

definition: Too many small gaps to count.
examples: Light came through the innumerable chinks in the hovel wall.

definition: Savagery and cruelty.
examples: The Creature suffers “the barbarity of man”.

definition: Morally good and pure.
examples: The De Lacey family seem virtuous and kind.

definition: Lacking morals or goodness.
examples: The Creature learns that men can be base and cruel.

definition: A terrible stain or flaw.
examples: The Creature asks if he is “a blot upon the earth”.

definition: An ugly thing that ruins the world around it.
examples: The Creature calls himself “a blot upon the earth”.

definition: Abandoned.
examples: The Creature feels disowned by all men.

definition: A person who is terrible, poor and unfortunate.
examples: Victor calls the Creature a “wretch”.

definition: Unsure.
examples: The Creature is irresolute before he enters the cottage.

definition: Abandoned.
examples: Victor deserted his creation on the night of its birth.

definition: Kind and friendly.
examples: The Creature hopes the family are amiable.

definition: Give up hope.
examples: The Creature falls into despair after being rejected.

definition: A person who supports someone who needs help.
examples: The Creature secretly acts as the De Laceys’ benefactor by gathering wood.

definition: Alarmed or worried.
examples: The family react with “horror and consternation”.

definition: Kindness.
examples: The Creature’s benevolence turns to hatred after he is rejected.

definition: Revenge.
examples: The Creature swears vengeance on Victor.

definition: Has no prejudices, will treat him fairly and kindly.
examples: The Creature thinks William will be unprejudiced.

definition: Swallowed, taken in.
examples: The Creature has imbibed hatred from the way people treat him.

definition: Lonely and deserted.
examples: Victor is left desolate by the deaths of those he loves.

definition: An ugly monster in fairytales.
examples: William shouts “You are an ogre!”

definition: Called me horrible names.
examples: William loaded the Creature with epithets.

definition: Show each other kindness and love.
examples: The Creature wants an interchange of sympathies with a companion.

definition: Obstacles that cannot be overcome.
examples: The Creature feels insurmountable barriers separate him from humanity.

definition: Allow myself to become a hopeless slave.
examples: The Creature refuses “the submission of abject slavery”.

definition: It will never die.
examples: The Creature’s hatred seems inextinguishable.

definition: Faces.
examples: The Creature studies the countenances of the De Laceys.

definition: A heartfelt plea to God.
examples: The Creature’s supplication goes unanswered.

definition: Disgusting and hated.
examples: The Creature feels abhorred by everyone he meets.

definition: A better representation of my life.
examples: The Creature calls Satan “the fitter emblem of my condition”.

definition: When an innocent person is punished or a criminal escapes punishment.
examples: Justine’s execution is a miscarriage of justice because the court assumed she was guilty before hearing the evidence.

definition: The organisations that create justice in society and punish wrongdoers (the police, courts and prisons).
examples: The justice system fails Justine, who is working-class and relies on it for protection.

definition: Something that is fair (fairness). (noun)
examples: Justine is denied justice because the court condemns her before hearing the evidence.

definition: Something that is not fair (unfairness). (noun)
examples: Justine’s execution is a terrible injustice.

definition: Describes something that is not fair. (adjective)
examples: Shelley shows an unjust society when Justine is executed.

definition: Describes something that is fair. (adjective)
examples: A just court would have listened to the evidence before judging Justine.

definition: The qualities that make someone human (love, kindness, sympathy).
examples: A monster has no humanity.
Someone without any humanity is a monster.
Victor thinks his creation has no humanity.
Elizabeth shows her humanity when she feels love and sympathy for Justine.
